Pool boiling heat transfer of saturated water on rough surfaces with
the effect of roughening techniques

The effect of surface roughness on pool boiling heat transfer was experimentally investigated in the saturated water. Eight testing surfaces were fabricated on plain copper through three preparation methods including random polishing, unidirectional polishing, and femtosecond laser machining. The surface
roughness in the present study is characterized by the areal (three dimensional, 3D) roughness parameter. In the two dimensional (2D) profile roughness analysis, we know that a profile can be separated into
the large-scale component (waviness) and the short-scale component (roughness). The arithmetical mean
height of the profile, the waviness and the roughness are denoted as Pa, Wa , and Ra , respectively. However, there are no such kind of parameters defined in the 3D roughness analysis. To distinguish them, we
define Sa p and Sa in this study, corresponding to Pa and Ra in the 2D roughness parameters. The pool
boiling experiments show that a rougher surface has higher heat transfer coefficient than a smoother
one only within the same surface preparation method, if the surface roughness is characterized by Sa p .
For the surfaces prepared by the different techniques, the laser processed rough surface with Sa p = 3 . 40
μm could have deteriorated heat transfer coefficient compared with the relatively smooth one polished
by the 180 grit sandpaper with Sa p = 1 . 29 μm. However, the different trend is observed when the surface
roughness is characterized by Sa . By applying a standardized filtration process, the large-scale component
of the surface can be removed, and the areal arithmetical mean height calculated from the remaining part
is denoted as Sa . The boiling curves are found to shift monotonically to the left as Sa becomes larger, re-
gardless of the surface preparation methods. The enhancement in heat transfer coefficient of rougher surfaces is attributed to a combined result of larger nucleation sites, smaller departure bubbles and higher
bubble departure frequencies, according to the visualization study. On the other hand, the critical heat
flux (CHF) does not show a clear trend with the surface roughness when the different surface preparation methods are involved, no matter Sa p or Sa is used. The measurements of static contact angle infer
that the CHF is not only dependent on surface roughness, but also highly related to surface wettability. A
correlation is developed to well predict the heat transfer coefficient from the experiments as a function
of Sa , especially in the fully developed nucleate boiling region.

1. Introduction
Pool boiling, as a passive two-phase cooling method, is expected to be a solution for the thermal management of devices
with high heat dissipation rate. The basic heat removal mechanism of pool boiling is so-called bubble nucleation, which is found
to highly depend on the surface-coolant interaction. The effects of
surface characteristics on pool boiling have attracted a lot of atten-

providing more nucleation sites and/or larger effective heat transfer area [1-4] . Therefore, the surface roughness is normally characterized by arithmetic mean roughness Ra or effective heat transfer area ratio r (the ratio of the actual heat transfer area and its

ically investigated the pool boiling heat transfer performance on
surfaces with the effective heat transfer area ratio r ranging from
1.79 to 5.94. Based on their experimental results, the CHF increased
monotonously with r due to roughness-amplified capillary pumping. On the other hand, the heat transfer coefficient did not show
a clear trend with r . Moita et al. [6] also found that surfaces with
larger r could not assure a higher boiling heat transfer coefficient.
They demonstrated that larger r could indeed increase the liquidsolid contact area, hence improving the heat transfer coefficient.
However, sometimes it also caused the early formation of vapor
blanket due to the severe interaction mechanism and coalescence
effect of the nucleation bubbles. This phenomenon would deteriorate the heat transfer coefficient and even overcome the bene-
fits of the increased liquid-solid contact area. Compared to the effective heat transfer area ratio r , the arithmetic mean roughness
Ra is used more frequently to characterize the surface roughness.
Many researchers visualized increased number of nucleation sites
on surfaces with larger Ra , which is believed responsible for the
enhancement of heat transfer coefficient [3,7,8] . However, some
different observations are also reported. Benjamin and Balakrishnan [9] found the number of nucleation sites was not consistently
increased with Ra . It decreased at first and then increased, as the
Ra became larger. Kozitskii [10] indicated that the nucleation boiling heat transfer coefficient increased with larger Ra up to a point
( Ra = 0 . 95 μm), beyond which no improvement occurred. Similar
trend was also reported by Jabardo [11] and El-Genk and Suszko
[12] .
The major obstacle to fully understand the effects of surface
roughness on pool boiling comes from the large variances in the
reported data. Generally, these inconsistent experimental data are
considered as a result of various surface roughening techniques,
roughness measurement uncertainties and different experimental
conditions such as working fluid, surface material and surface wettability. Jones et al. [7] conducted pool boiling experiments to investigate the effect of surface roughness on a aluminum surface
in water and FC-77 respectively. They observed totally different
effects of the surface roughness on the heat transfer coefficient
in the two working fluids, even though the other experimental
conditions were controlled the same. Kim and his group studied
the effect of surface roughness on pool boiling heat transfer on
a superhydrophilic [8] , a moderate-wetted [4] and a hydrophobic
surface [13] , respectively. On the superhydrophilic and moderatewetted surfaces, the nucleate boiling heat transfer coefficient was
enhanced as the surface roughness increased, even though several
cases exhibited deviation from the overall trends. However, the experiments on the hydrophobic surface showed totally different re-
sults. On the hydrophobic surface, the nucleate boiling heat transfer coefficient of a rougher surface was initially higher than that of
a smoother one but decreased rapidly to a very low value in moderate and high heat flux regime, leading to an early occurrence of
CHF. They explained that such trend was a result of the early formation of vapor blanket on the hydrophobic surface, same as that
demonstrated by Moita et al. [6] .
The surface roughening techniques are essential in studying the
roughness effects on pool boiling. Researchers have emphasized
that the surface roughness is meaningless without specifying the
surface roughening technique. Berenson [14] found the lapped surface had higher heat transfer coefficient than the emery-polished
one, although the lapped surface was smoother. Vachon et al.
[15] prepared surfaces by unidirectionally polishing and chemically
etching. The heat transfer coefficients of surfaces with these two
surface roughening techniques were different even though the Rq
(root-mean-square roughness) was similar. Other researchers also
pointed out the necessity of using a consistent surface roughening technique when studying the effect of surface roughness on
pool boiling [16,17] . The reason is that surfaces prepared by some
roughening techniques have higher tendency to bubble nucleation,
regardless of the surface roughness. Besides, the standardized surface roughness parameters, such as Ra and Rq , are statistical average values which cannot indicate the actual surface texture, especially the number of nucleation cavities. A smooth surface indicated by small Ra or Rq can also have a lot of cavities for nucleation. Many researchers reported the inadequacy of using an
individual statistical parameter to characterize the surface roughness for pool boiling [2,15,17,18] . In fact, Berenson believed that a
"rougher" surface in pool boiling should be that has more cavities
necessary for nucleation, but not the one with a larger value of Ra
or Rq . Some researchers developed methods to measure the surface
active cavity size, in order to determine the potential nucleation
sites quantitatively [19-22] . However, their methods are based on
the simplistic treatment of the surface texture and wetting phenomenon. The accurate quantitative prediction of the nucleation
sites is still unrealizable. Researchers still need to characterize the
surface roughness with the aid of standardized roughness parameters.
The present study aims to investigate the effect of surface
roughness on copper surfaces. The experiments were conducted
in the saturated water at atmospheric pressure. A total of eight
testing surfaces were prepared by three different surface roughening techniques, respectively. The different surface roughening techniques can introduce different f eatures of surface texture. These
features can be effectively eliminated by applying a novel pre-
processing method before surface roughness measurement. The
trends in the nucleate boiling heat transfer coefficient and CHF
were discussed and the bubble dynamics was studied using a high

2. Experimental setup and procedures
2.1. Experimental setup
The schematic diagram of the experimental setup is shown in
Fig. 1 (a). The whole apparatus consists of a boiling chamber, a testing part, a temperature measurement system and a visualization
system. The boiling chamber has a transparent side wall and top
cover made of Acrylic in order to perform visualization study. The
base plate of the boiling chamber is made of Teflon for the thermal insulation purpose. Experiments were conducted in this chamber using distilled water under atmospheric pressure. A pressure
gauge is connected to the chamber in order to monitor the inter-
nal pressure. A copper coil, together with water bath, is performed
as a vapor condenser. The condenser is able to condense the vapor
generated in the chamber and maintain the liquid level constant.
Four immersion heaters are installed inside the boiling chamber
to provide heat to the liquid. These immersion heaters are connected to a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller, which
can control the liquid temperature by detecting it with a K-type
thermocouple. In this experiment, the liquid temperature is kept at
around 99.5 ◦C, which is the saturation temperature at atmospheric
pressure. In the testing part, a copper block is surrounded by the
thermal insulation material. The testing surface on the top of the
copper block has a dimension of 20 × 20 mm 2 . The copper block
is heated by four heaters with the capability of providing a maximum heat flux of 150 W/cm 2 . Three thermocouples with hot junction diameter of 0.5 mm are aligned 4 mm, 10 mm and 16 mm
from the testing surface in the center of the copper block with
holes of 0.6 mm, as shown in Fig. 1 (b). During the experiments,
the bubbles were prior to generate at the edge of the testing surface. Methods of eliminating the edge nucleation sites had been
performed. The one shown in Fig. 1 is proved to efficiently reduce
the edge nucleation sites. The space between the copper and the
teflon holder is first filled with RTV sealant and then covered by a
fluidic thermal insulation material 3M Epoxy DP 460. There is still
nucleation sites at the edge using this method due to the different
thermal expansion rate of the copper, RTV sealant and the epoxy.
But this method could effectively reduce the number of the edge
nucleation sites to an acceptable range. The temperature measurement system includes four K-type thermocouples, a data acquisition system (Agilent 34972A LXI Data acquisition Unit) and a computer. All the thermocouples were calibrated using a dry block calibrator (Techne Ucal 400+) with an accuracy of 0.2 ◦C. The visualization system includes a LED light source (Leica CLS150 LED), a
high speed camera (Fastec Imaging HiSpec 2G Mono) and a computer. Bubbles at the boiling surface were captured and recorded
by the visualization system at a frame rate of 20 0 0fps during the
experiments.
2.2. Surface preparation
The modified surfaces in this experiment were prepared by two
different methods. Before applying the surface preparation methods, the surface was first randomly polished with 2400 grit sandpaper (Struers Silicon Carbide Grinding Paper) and cleaned by sonicating in distilled water. The treated surface served as base surface in the experiment. The base surface was then roughened by
unidirectional polishing with rougher sandpapers (80, 120, 180,
60 0, and 120 0 grit) or femtosecond laser processing. A total of
eight samples were prepared, including five unidirectionally polished surfaces, two laser processed surfaces and a base surface
as reference. Two important surface characteristics, surface roughness and static contact angle, were measured on the testing surfaces. The surface roughness was measured by a 3D optical surface metrology system, Leica DCM-8. The measurement results are

As shown in Fig. 3 , Fig. 3 (a) is the raw measured surface. It can
be found that some bad points compress the surface dynamic, impeding us from obtaining detained information on the surface. This
can be seen more clearly on the depth distribution of the measured surface ( Fig. 3 (b)). A few number of deep holes covers most
of the depth range (from 20.3 μm to 50.9 μm), while the main
body of the surface (over 99.9% number of point) locates only at
0-20.3 μm. This phenomenon is an inherent drawback of the non-
contact instrument, as explained by the manufacturer. A spatial filter operator, with a median denoising filter 3 × 3, could eliminate
the bad points (Step 1). The surface is then leveled by subtracting
the least square plane from the whole surface area (Step 2). The
leveled surface ( Fig. 3 (d)) is a rectangular one. A square area is extracted from the leveled surface for better analysis (Step 3). During the measurement, some data points were not measured due to
various reasons. These missing points are filled in using a smooth
shape calculated from the neighboring points (Step 4). After that,
a median smoothing filter 7 × 7 is applied to the surface in order to eliminate noise and improve image quality (Step 5). For surface texture, there are two geometrical product specifications published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO),
i.e., ISO 4287 and ISO 25178. The ISO 4287 specifies the terms, definitions and surface texture parameters based on profile method
(2D), while the ISO 25178 collects the international standards re-
lating to surface texture based on areal method (3D). The denoised
surface after Step 5 can be treated as the S-F surface in ISO 25178,

which is a surface obtained after applying an F-operator (a filter
to correct tilt and suppress the nominal surface texture characterization). The areal primary parameters Sa p (corresponds to Pa in
ISO 4287) and the effective heat transfer area ratio r can be calculated from this surface. As shown in Fig. 3 (g), the S-F surface
still consists of long wavelength component (waviness) and short
wavelength component (roughness). For pool boiling, the waviness
part is obviously too large for nucleation cavities which are only
in micro-scale. Therefore, the denoised surface is split into waviness components ( Fig. 3 (h)) and roughness components ( Fig. 3 (i)),
by applying an areal robust gaussian filter with a cut-off of 25
μm. The surface roughness parameters are then calculated from the
roughness components ( Fig. 3 (i)) according to ISO 25178 standard.
In the filtration process, selecting appropriate cut-off value (the
limit wavelength between the long-scale component and short-
scale component) is critical in order to separate roughness from
waviness properly. There is not a generally accepted criterion for
determining the cut-off value, especially for the areal filter. The
choice of cut-off value is very empirical and highly dependent
on the practical application. In present study, the cut-off is determined as a result of many attempts, and a cut-off value of 25
μm is finally selected in order to assure that the irrelevant long-
scale component is well removed and the short-scale component
which has similar magnitude with the nucleation cavities can be
remained as much as possible, as shown in Fig. 4 . In the ISO 25178
standard, both the areal arithmetical mean height calculated from
Fig. 3 (g) and that calculated from Fig. 3 (i) are denoted as Sa . To
distinguish them, the former one is denoted as Sa p in this study.

ferent surface preparation methods. The static contact angle of the
laser processed surfaces is much larger than that of the sandpaper
polished surfaces. For the polished surfaces, the static contact angle initially increases with surface roughness and remains a constant for further increase in surface roughness. This relationship
between the static contact angle and the surface roughness is different from the results reported in previous literature [13,23,24] .
The specific surface topography in the experiment can be a possible reason of this trend. As we know, the static contact angle
highly depends on the spreading effect of the sessile drop on the
testing surfaces. Rougher surface with larger scratches could obstruct droplet from spreading on the surface, especially in the direction normal to the scratches. Therefore, the static contact angle
is increased as the surface becomes rougher. This increase does not
occur anymore when the surface roughness Sa is larger than 0.57
μm. Beyond which, the obstruction effect of the droplet spreading has encountered a threshold value. Further increase in surface roughness will not cause the surface more hydrophobic. On
the other hand, for the femtosecond laser processed surfaces, the
static contact angles of both surfaces were around 153 ◦. The surface roughness had negligible effect on the static contact angle.
2.3. Experimental procedures
The boiling chamber was filled with distilled water to a level
about 150 mm above the testing surface. Before the experiment,
the water was first heated up by the immersion heaters and boiled
for around one hour in order to release the non-condensable gases.
After degassing, the PID controller was set to 99.5 ◦C and the liquid was maintained at saturation state. Once the internal pressure
8
S. Fan, L. Jiao and K. Wang et al. / International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer 159 (2020) 120054
and liquid temperature got stabilized, a settled voltage was applied
to the test heaters. The wall temperature would experience an initial increase and gradually reach steady state. In this experiment,
we considered the wall temperature became stable when the variation of the thermocouple measurement in the cooper block was
less than 0.2 ◦C within one minute. The temperatures were calculated by averaging 30 measured values in the steady state. Bubble
dynamics in the steady state were also recorded by the visualization system. The voltage was then increased to next predetermined
value and the same recording procedure was repeated until the occurrence of a sudden increase of the measured temperature (temperature of the copper block increased over 20 ◦C in one minute).
Once the abrupt increase occurred, the power to the test heaters
must be shut down immediately in order to protect the boiling
surface from burnout. The critical heat flux (CHF) was determined
as the heat flux just before the sudden increase of the measured
temperature. It is a remarkable fact that all the experiments were
conducted once the surfaces had been prepared. The aging effect
of surfaces is not considered in present study. Additional studies
on the roughness effects of pool boiling as a function of time will
be performed in our future work.

3. Results and discussion
To validate the results of the present experiments, the experimental data of the reference surface ( Sa = 0.045 μm) are compared
with previous studies which are performed in similar experimental conditions, i.e., saturated water pool boiling on smooth copper
surface at atmosphere pressure. As shown in Fig. 6 , the present
experimental results are almost overlapped with the data from Jun
et al. [26] and Yang et al. [27] . However, some discrepancy is observed in the study of other researchers [28-30] . This is because
that nucleate boiling is such a complicated process which includes
a lot of influence factors. The difference in any influence factor,
measurement accuracy and data processing method can be a possible reason of the discrepancy. Generally, the present experimental data is quite comparable with the previous studies. Besides the
previous data, the well-known Rohsenow correlation is also plotted in Fig. 6 . The correlation was derived by Rohsenow in 1951 and
was widely applied for predicting nucleate boiling heat transfer of
saturated pool boiling [31] .

The visualization studies of all the testing surfaces under a
same heat flux are shown in Fig. 9 and the supplementary animation. For a certain testing surface, there is a larger number of
nucleation bubbles as the heat flux increases. This explains why
the nucleate boiling heat transfer coefficient h increases with the
increasing heat flux q . It can be also found that the number of nucleation bubbles always increases with the roughness parameter Sa
at a certain heat flux. However, it should be noted that the relation between roughness parameter Sa and number of nucleation
sites is only a qualitative observation. Quantitative description of
the potential nucleation sites can be received by size distribution

researchers [19,21] . The details will not be discussed here due to
limited length. A simple quantitative analysis of bubble departure
diameter and bubble departure frequency is conducted using the
image processing program ImageJ. The results are shown in Fig. 10 .
Three surfaces with totally different surface roughening techniques
and surface roughness parameters are included in the analysis. The

4. Conclusions
The effect of surface roughness on the nucleate boiling heat
transfer in a water pool was investigated. The copper surfaces
used in the experiments were fabricated by three different surface
roughening techniques (unidirectionally polished, randomly polished and laser processed) and had an average roughness in the
range of 0.045 μm to 1.35 μm. The different surface roughening
techniques could introduce different surface features and surface
wettability. Bubble dynamics was also investigated to further understand the nucleate boiling heat transfer. Based on the results
and discussion, the following conclusions were deduced:
• The unidirectionally polished surface had a lot of irregular scratches, while the femtosecond laser processed samples
showed periodically fluctuating surface texture. For the sandpaper polished surfaces, the contact angle initially increased
with surface roughness and remained a constant as the surface roughness further increased. The trend was a result of
the spreading effect of the sessile droplet on the testing surfaces. Rougher surface with larger scratches could obstruct the
droplet from spreading on the surface, especially in the direction normal to the scratches. Therefore, the static contact angle was increased as the surface became rougher. This increase
did not occur anymore when the surface roughness Sa was
larger than 0.57 μm. Beyond which, the obstruction effect of the
droplet spreading had encountered a threshold value. A further
increase in surface roughness would not cause the surface more
hydrophobic. On the other hand, for the femtosecond laser processed surfaces, the static contact angles of both surfaces were
around 153 ◦. The surface roughness had negligible effect on the
static contact angle.
• By applying a standardized filtration process on the measured
surfaces, the boiling curves were found to shift to the left as
the surface roughness parameter Sa became larger, regardless of
the surface preparation method. The surface roughening technique had negligible effect on the nucleate boiling heat transfer coefficient once the large scale surface texture (surface form
and waviness) were properly removed from the surface. On the
other hand, the CHF was affected by both the surface roughness
and surface roughening technique. It is not a monotonic function of surface roughness without specifying the surface roughening technique. The surface wettability also played an important role in determining the CHF.
• The rough surfaces enhanced the nucleate boiling heat transfer
by providing more nucleation sites, decreasing bubble departure diameter and increasing bubble departure frequency. Besides, the number of nucleation bubbles was found to increase
with heat flux, which well explained that the heat transfer co-
efficient is an increasing function of heat flux in all boiling
curves.
• A correlation was developed based on the best fitting of the
experimental data. The validation results showed that the correlation was able to well predict the heat transfer coefficient at
different surface roughness Sa , especially in the fully developed
nucleate boiling region.
